name: Birefringent phase matching and electro-optic χ(2)
summary: Crystal birefringence makes efficient harmonic generation possible: picking the propagation angle so that n_e(2ω,θ)=n_o(ω) gives Δk=0 (type-I phase matching). The Pockels and Kerr electro-optic effects of crystal optics are χ(2)(ω;ω,0) and χ(3)(ω;ω,0,0) with a DC field; the lithium-niobate r_33 coefficient drives Mach–Zehnder modulators.
sources: Franken et al. (1961). "Generation of Optical Harmonics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 7, 118. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118)

name: Gyrotropy: magneto-optic non-reciprocity enables one-way modes
summary: Faraday rotation comes from an imaginary antisymmetric off-diagonal permittivity or permeability (gyrotropy) induced by a magnetic field. This breaks reciprocity, which is why optical isolators work. Gyromagnetic photonic crystals use the same broken time-reversal symmetry to open bands with nonzero Chern number, giving the first one-way photonic edge states (Haldane–Raghu proposal, microwave YIG experiment).
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Radiation reaction: the Abraham–Lorentz–Dirac force
summary: The energy and momentum carried off by Larmor radiation imply a self-force on the charge. Dirac's covariant derivation from the retarded-minus-advanced self-field gives the Abraham–Lorentz–Dirac equation, which reduces to the Abraham–Lorentz force at low speed.
breaks: The ALD equation has runaway and pre-acceleration solutions. In practice the reduced-order Landau–Lifshitz form is used, valid when the force changes slowly over r_e/c.
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)

name: Lorentz–Drude ε(ω), Kramers–Kronig and skin depth
summary: The frequency-dependent response from fields in matter, with bound electrons as damped Lorentz oscillators and free electrons as the ω0=0 Drude case, determines how waves propagate. It sets dispersion, absorption lines, the plasma frequency below which metals reflect, and the skin depth. Causality links Re ε and Im ε through Kramers–Kronig.

name: Optical fibres and chips as dielectric waveguides
summary: Fibre and on-chip guides are solved with the same Maxwell boundary-value problem as microwave waveguides: guided modes, cutoffs, group-velocity dispersion and coupled-mode theory. Confinement comes from total internal reflection at an index step instead of metal walls, and a step-index fibre is single-mode for V<2.405.
breaks: Unlike a hollow metal guide, the fundamental mode of a dielectric guide has no cutoff, and its field reaches evanescently into the cladding, which allows bend loss and evanescent coupling.
sources: Kao & Hockham (1966). "Dielectric-fibre surface waveguides for optical frequencies". *Proc. IEE* 113, 1151. [doi:10.1049/piee.1966.0189](https://doi.org/10.1049/piee.1966.0189)

name: Surface plasmon polaritons as bound TM interface waves
summary: Maxwell's equations with Fresnel boundary conditions at a metal–dielectric interface admit a bound TM surface wave whenever ε_m<−ε_d; it is the pole of the p-polarized reflection coefficient. Combined with the Drude permittivity and conductor skin depth, this gives the SPP dispersion, sub-wavelength confinement and propagation loss.

name: Refractive index as coherent forward scattering
summary: By the Ewald–Oseen extinction theorem, radiation from the induced dipoles cancels the incident wave inside a medium and replaces it with a wave of phase velocity c/n. The index follows from the forward scattering amplitude, and the optical theorem ties its imaginary part to extinction, i.e. attenuation.
breaks: The simple formula holds for dilute media (|n−1|≪1). Dense media need local-field (Lorentz–Lorenz) corrections.

name: Transformation optics: form-invariance of Maxwell's equations
summary: Maxwell's equations keep their form under any coordinate map if ε and μ are replaced by transformed tensors. A desired light path, such as one bending around a hole, thus becomes a material prescription. Cloaks, concentrators and illusion devices are designed this way and built from metamaterials.
breaks: Ideal cloaks need singular, anisotropic and dispersive parameters, so causality restricts them to narrow bands and approximate versions. Eikonal-only (ray) cloaks relax these requirements.

name: Maxwell's master equation as a topological band problem
summary: In a lossless periodic medium Maxwell's equations become a Hermitian eigenproblem for H. Photonic Bloch modes therefore carry Berry connections and Chern numbers just as electron bands do, which lets band topology, bulk–edge correspondence and one-way edge waveguides carry over to optics.
breaks: Photons are bosons with no Fermi level, so there is no quantized transport response. Gain, loss and material dispersion make the problem non-Hermitian or require auxiliary fields.
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Synthetic gauge fields: Peierls phases for neutral photons
summary: Photons carry no charge, but engineered direction-dependent hopping phases in coupled-resonator or waveguide lattices play the role of (q/ħ)∫A·dl. They create an effective magnetic flux per plaquette and photonic Harper–Hofstadter bands with quantum-Hall-like edge states.
breaks: The synthetic potential is static and non-dynamical: there is no Lorentz force on a free photon and no gauge redundancy acting on matter. Pseudospin schemes keep time-reversal symmetry, so disorder that mixes pseudospins causes backscattering.
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Liénard–Wiechert = retarded Lorenz-gauge potentials
summary: The Liénard–Wiechert potentials are the retarded solutions of the Lorenz-gauge wave equations for a point charge. The factor 1/(1−n·β), which comes from evaluating the delta function at retarded time, produces relativistic beaming and the γ^4 growth of synchrotron loss.

name: Magnetism as electrostatics plus relativity
summary: In the rest frame of a charge moving beside a current-carrying wire, the magnetic force becomes an electric force from Lorentz-contracted, unbalanced line charges. The field-strength tensor makes E and B one object, and the field of a uniformly moving charge has B=v×E/c², which reduces to Biot–Savart at low speed.
map: \mathbf E'_\perp=\gamma(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)_\perp,\quad \mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf v\times\mathbf E}{c^2}\ \text{(uniformly moving charge)}
breaks: The derivation takes charge invariance and Lorentz covariance as inputs. Intrinsic magnetic moments (spin) do not come from moving charges.

name: Liénard's formula: the Lorentz-invariant Larmor power
summary: Radiated power is a Lorentz scalar, so the non-relativistic Larmor formula fixes its covariant form in terms of the four-acceleration. This gives Liénard's γ^6 result and the γ^4/R^2 synchrotron loss, and aberration of the rest-frame dipole pattern gives the 1/γ beaming cone.
sources: Schwinger (1949). "On the Classical Radiation of Accelerated Electrons". *Phys. Rev.* 75, 1912. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.75.1912](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.75.1912)

name: Localized plasmons: poles of the electrostatic sphere
summary: The quasi-static sphere polarizability diverges at the Fröhlich condition ε_m(ω)=−2ε_d, which is the localized surface plasmon resonance of metal nanoparticles (ω_p/√3 for a Drude metal in vacuum). In the electrostatic limit Pendry's perfect lens needs only ε=−1, so Laplace-equation solutions are used to design near-field plasmonics.
breaks: Loss (Im ε_m) caps the resonance. For particles beyond about λ/10, radiation damping and retardation red-shift and broaden it, and below about 2 nm nonlocal and quantum response shifts it.
sources: Pendry (2000). "Negative Refraction Makes a Perfect Lens". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 3966. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966)

name: Rayleigh scattering from the electrostatic dielectric sphere
summary: A particle much smaller than λ sees a quasi-static field, so its induced dipole is that of a dielectric sphere in a uniform field, solved by Legendre separation of Laplace's equation. Radiating this dipole gives the ω^4 Rayleigh cross section with the same (ε−1)/(ε+2) factor.
breaks: The quasi-static picture fails once ka or |m|ka is no longer small. Retardation, magnetic dipoles and higher multipoles then enter (the Mie regime).

name: Designer ε(ω) and μ(ω) by homogenization
summary: Metamaterials apply the macroscopic-field averaging of fields in matter (microscopic dipoles → P, M → ε, μ) to artificial sub-wavelength 'atoms'. Split rings give a resonant magnetization and wire arrays a Drude-like ε, so both can be made negative. Maxwell Garnett mixing is the Clausius–Mossotti relation applied to inclusions.
breaks: Homogenization needs cells ≪λ. Real metamaterial cells are only λ/5–λ/10, so spatial dispersion, bianisotropy and loss leave ε and μ only approximately defined.
sources: Pendry (2000). "Negative Refraction Makes a Perfect Lens". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 3966. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966)

name: Multipole expansion of radiating sources
summary: The static multipole hierarchy carries over to time-harmonic sources: for ka≪1 the radiation field is a series of electric and magnetic multipoles, each order suppressed by about (ka)^2 relative to the one before, with electric-dipole radiation leading. The spherical harmonics of the static expansion become the vector spherical harmonics of the radiation pattern.
map: \langle P_{E1}\rangle=\frac{\mu_0\omega^4|\mathbf p|^2}{12\pi c},\ P_{M1}:\ \mathbf p\to\mathbf m/c,\ P_{\ell+1}/P_\ell\sim(ka)^2

name: Mie theory as a multipole expansion
summary: Mie's exact solution for a sphere expands the scattered field in vector spherical harmonics: electric (a_n) and magnetic (b_n) multipoles of rising order. Rayleigh scattering is the leading electric-dipole term, and the number of multipoles needed grows with the size parameter x=ka.
sources: Mie (1908). "Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen". *Ann. Phys.* 330, 377. [doi:10.1002/andp.19083300302](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19083300302)

name: Free-electron lasers: stimulated undulator radiation
summary: An FEL turns the spontaneous undulator radiation of relativistic electrons into laser light. The ponderomotive coupling between the beam and the co-propagating field microbunches the electrons at the resonant wavelength, so emission becomes coherent and grows exponentially without population inversion of bound states.
breaks: The gain is a collective classical bunching instability, not inversion between discrete levels. SASE output starts from shot noise and has poor temporal coherence unless seeded.

name: Inhibited and enhanced emission: dipoles in engineered LDOS
summary: The power a dipole radiates depends on its surroundings through the local density of states, i.e. the imaginary part of the Green's function at the source. Photonic band gaps suppress emission (Yablonovitch), while cavities and plasmonic nanoantennas enhance it (Purcell). A radio antenna's radiation resistance shifts near reflectors for the same reason.
map: \frac{P}{P_0}=\frac{6\pi c}{\omega}\hat{\mathbf p}\cdot\mathrm{Im}\,\mathbf G(\mathbf r_0,\mathbf r_0)\cdot\hat{\mathbf p},\quad F_P=\frac{3}{4\pi^2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^3\frac{Q}{V}
sources: Yablonovitch (1987). "Inhibited Spontaneous Emission in Solid-State Physics and Electronics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 2059. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059)

name: Stimulated Raman and Brillouin scattering
summary: Spontaneous Raman scattering (molecular vibrations) and Brillouin scattering (acoustic phonons) turn stimulated at high intensity. The pump–Stokes beat drives the material excitation coherently, giving exponential Stokes gain through the imaginary part of the resonant χ(3). SBS limits the power of narrow-linewidth fibre lasers.

name: Coherent backscattering is weak localization
summary: In a disordered medium each multiple-scattering path interferes constructively with its time-reversed partner in the exact backward direction, doubling the reflected intensity in a cone of width ~λ/ℓ*; this is the optical twin of the weak-localization correction to electrical conductance and a precursor of Anderson localization.
sources: Wolf & Maret (1985). "Weak Localization and Coherent Backscattering of Photons in Disordered Media". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2696. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2696](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2696)

van Albada & Lagendijk (1985). "Observation of Weak Localization of Light in a Random Medium". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2692. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2692](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2692)

name: Thermal light: Bose–Einstein fluctuations and bunching
summary: A single mode of thermal light has a geometric Bose–Einstein photon-number distribution with variance n̄ + n̄². The n̄² wave term is classical interference of random phasors (Gaussian statistics, g⁽²⁾(0) = 2, Hanbury Brown–Twiss bunching); the n̄ term is particle shot noise. Together they are Einstein's 1909 fluctuation formula for blackbody radiation.
map: P(n)=\frac{\bar n^n}{(1+\bar n)^{n+1}},\qquad \langle\Delta n^2\rangle=\bar n+\bar n^2,\qquad g^{(2)}(\tau)=1+|g^{(1)}(\tau)|^2
sources: Glauber (1963). "The Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 2529. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529)
Mandel & Wolf (1995). "Optical Coherence and Quantum Optics". Cambridge University Press. [doi:10.1017/cbo9781139644105](https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139644105)

name: Wiener–Khinchin: spectra from correlation functions
summary: The optical power spectrum is the Fourier transform of the field autocorrelation (Wiener–Khinchin), the same relation that defines noise spectral densities in linear-response theory; the FDT then ties the spectrum of thermal light to the absorptive response of the emitter.
map: S(\omega)=\int\langle E^*(t)E(t+\tau)\rangle e^{i\omega\tau}d\tau\ \leftrightarrow\ S_x(\omega)=\int\langle x(t)x(0)\rangle e^{i\omega t}dt
sources: Mandel & Wolf (1995). "Optical Coherence and Quantum Optics". Cambridge University Press. [doi:10.1017/cbo9781139644105](https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139644105)

name: Speckle as a random walk of phasors
summary: A speckle field is a sum of many phasors with random phases, a two-dimensional random walk, so by the central limit theorem it is a circular Gaussian field with exponential intensity statistics and unit contrast. Pearson posed the random-walk problem in 1905 and Rayleigh answered it from his theory of superposed vibrations of random phase.
map: A=\sum_{k=1}^Na_ke^{i\phi_k}\ \Rightarrow\ p(I)=\frac{1}{\langle I\rangle}e^{-I/\langle I\rangle},\qquad C=\frac{\sigma_I}{\langle I\rangle}=1
sources: Goodman (1976). "Some fundamental properties of speckle". *J. Opt. Soc. Am.* 66, 1145. [doi:10.1364/JOSA.66.001145](https://doi.org/10.1364/JOSA.66.001145)
Pearson (1905). "The Problem of the Random Walk". *Nature* 72, 294. [doi:10.1038/072294b0](https://doi.org/10.1038/072294b0)

name: Maximum-entropy image reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing an image from incomplete Fourier data (interferometer visibilities, blurred noisy images) is underdetermined; choosing the image of maximum entropy consistent with the data within the noise is Jaynes's MaxEnt inference transplanted to imaging, a standard deconvolution method in radio astronomy.
sources: Gull & Daniell (1978). "Image reconstruction from incomplete and noisy data". *Nature* 272, 686. [doi:10.1038/272686a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/272686a0)
Jaynes (1957). "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev.* 106, 620. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.106.620](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.106.620)

name: Étendue conservation and the brightness theorem
summary: Étendue n²A dΩ is the phase-space volume of a ray bundle and is conserved by any passive optical system (Liouville), so radiance cannot be increased and no lens or mirror can heat a target above the Sun's surface temperature; this is the second law in ray optics and fixes the maximum solar concentration n²/sin²θ_s.

name: Cavity mode counting and the Planck law
summary: The density of electromagnetic standing-wave modes in a cavity, 8πν²/c³, times the mean energy per mode gives the blackbody spectrum: equipartition (k_BT per mode) yields Rayleigh–Jeans and the ultraviolet catastrophe, while Bose–Einstein occupation of each mode as a quantum oscillator yields Planck's law.
breaks: Weyl mode counting needs cavity size ≫ λ; in sub-wavelength cavities and photonic crystals the density of states is engineered and the free-space Planck law no longer applies.
sources: Planck (1901). "Ueber das Gesetz der Energieverteilung im Normalspectrum". *Ann. Phys.* 309, 553. [doi:10.1002/andp.19013090310](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19013090310)

name: Johnson–Nyquist noise from a 1D blackbody line
summary: Nyquist derived thermal voltage noise by letting two resistors exchange energy through a lossless transmission line whose modes each hold k_BT, a one-dimensional blackbody; this is the first fluctuation–dissipation theorem, generalized by Callen–Welton. The same physics sets antenna noise temperature, which is how the CMB was first read.
sources: Nyquist (1928). "Thermal Agitation of Electric Charge in Conductors". *Phys. Rev.* 32, 110. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.32.110](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.32.110)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)
Penzias & Wilson (1965). "A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s". *Astrophys. J.* 142, 419. [doi:10.1086/148307](https://doi.org/10.1086/148307)

name: Radiation pressure and the Stefan–Boltzmann law
summary: The Maxwell stress tensor gives isotropic radiation the pressure p = u/3; inserting this into the thermodynamic identity (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂p/∂T)_V − p forces u ∝ T⁴ (Boltzmann 1884), and the adiabatic invariant VT³ = const gives Wien's displacement law.
map: p=\frac u3,\quad \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T=T\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V-p\ \Rightarrow\ u=aT^4,\quad VT^3=\text{const (adiabatic)}

name: Bohr–van Leeuwen theorem: no classical magnetism
summary: With minimal coupling H(p − qA), the classical canonical partition function is independent of A after shifting the momentum integration, so classical statistical mechanics predicts zero equilibrium magnetization; diamagnetism and paramagnetism are quantum effects. Gauge invariance of the partition function is the formal content.
map: Z=\int d^3r\,d^3p\,e^{-\beta H(\mathbf r,\mathbf p-q\mathbf A)}\ \stackrel{\mathbf p\to\mathbf p+q\mathbf A}{=}\ Z|_{\mathbf A=0}\ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf M=-\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mathbf B}=0
sources: Müller et al. (2024). "Gauge Invariance of Equilibrium Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 133, 217101. [arXiv:2406.19235](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19235)

name: Poisson–Boltzmann and Debye–Hückel as mean-field electrostatics
summary: Closing Poisson's equation with Boltzmann-distributed ion densities gives the Poisson–Boltzmann equation, a mean-field theory of electrolytes and charged colloids; linearized it yields Debye–Hückel screening, and it fails (ion correlations, like-charge attraction) exactly where fluctuations beyond mean field matter.

name: Magnetocaloric effect and adiabatic demagnetization
summary: Adding the field work term μ₀H·dM (or E·dP) to the fundamental relation makes H and M a conjugate pair like −p and V; the resulting Maxwell relation gives the magnetocaloric and electrocaloric effects and adiabatic demagnetization, the classic route to millikelvin temperatures.
map: dG=-S\,dT-\mu_0M\,dH,\qquad \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial H}\right)_T=\mu_0\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\right)_H,\qquad \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial H}\right)_S=-\frac{\mu_0T}{C_H}\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\right)_H

name: Effective-medium theory and percolating composites
summary: The effective permittivity or conductivity of a metal–dielectric composite (Maxwell Garnett, Bruggeman) is a mean-field theory of a random network; Bruggeman's symmetric theory predicts a conductor–insulator threshold (p_c = 1/3 in 3D), and near the true percolation threshold metal films show power-law conductivity and giant local-field fluctuations.

name: Langevin–Debye orientational polarizability
summary: Permanent dipoles in a field have canonical weights e^{pE cosθ/k_BT}; averaging gives the Langevin function and, at weak field, the Debye orientational polarizability p²/3k_BT, the electric twin of Curie's law for paramagnets and the microscopic origin of temperature-dependent ε and χ.

name: Dielectric function as a causal response function
summary: ε(ω) and the Drude/Lorentz models are the archetypal linear-response functions: causality makes χ analytic in the upper half-plane, giving the Kramers–Kronig relations between refraction and absorption; Im ε measures dissipation, and Kubo's formula gives the optical conductivity from equilibrium current correlations.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Landau–Devonshire theory of ferroelectrics
summary: Spontaneous polarization in a ferroelectric is a Landau order parameter: expanding the free energy in P gives Curie–Weiss divergence of ε above T_c, hysteresis as metastable branches, and first- versus second-order transitions from the sign of the quartic term; ferromagnetic M and χ follow the same theory.

name: Shannon capacity limits of optical fibre
summary: Shannon's channel capacity bounds data rates in fibre networks; because Kerr nonlinearity makes noise grow with launch power, achievable spectral efficiency peaks at an optimum power (the nonlinear Shannon limit), tying information entropy to fibre physics.
sources: Shannon (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication". *Bell Syst. Tech. J.* 27, 379. [doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x)

name: The three-level maser as a Carnot engine
summary: A three-level maser pumped by a hot reservoir and relaxed by a cold one is a heat engine: each emitted photon converts heat to work with efficiency ν_s/ν_p, which population inversion forces to stay below the Carnot efficiency (Scovil and Schulz-DuBois 1959), the founding example of quantum heat engines.
sources: Scovil & Schulz-DuBois (1959). "Three-Level Masers as Heat Engines". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 2, 262. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.2.262](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.2.262)

name: Optical refrigeration and the entropy of light
summary: Anti-Stokes fluorescence cooling of solids removes heat by emitting broadband, isotropic fluorescence that carries more entropy than the narrow, collimated pump; Landau's entropy of radiation keeps the second law intact and bounds the cooling efficiency.

sources: Epstein et al. (1995). "Observation of laser-induced fluorescent cooling of a solid". *Nature* 377, 500. [doi:10.1038/377500a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/377500a0)

name: Chemical potential of light: photon BEC versus lasing
summary: When photons thermalize by repeated absorption and re-emission in a dye-filled microcavity, their number is conserved and they acquire a chemical potential; above a critical number they Bose-condense into the lowest cavity mode, distinct from lasing, which needs inversion. Luminescent radiation from LEDs and solar cells likewise carries μ = qV (Würfel's generalized Planck law).
sources: Klaers et al. (2010). "Bose–Einstein condensation of photons in an optical microcavity". *Nature* 468, 545. [arXiv:1007.4088](https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.4088)

name: Random and multimode lasers as photonic spin glasses
summary: Mode amplitudes of multimode lasers evolve under an effective Hamiltonian of four-mode couplings; with random couplings (random lasers) this is a spherical p-spin glass at an effective temperature set by noise over pump squared, and replica-symmetry breaking has been reported in shot-to-shot spectral fluctuations. Passive mode-locking is the ordered phase of the same theory.
breaks: Effective equilibrium holds only in a slow-amplitude mean-field limit; real lasers are open and dissipative, and the measured RSB overlaps are indirect.
sources: Ghofraniha et al. (2015). "Experimental evidence of replica symmetry breaking in random lasers". *Nature Commun.* 6, 6058. [doi:10.1038/ncomms7058](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms7058)
Parisi (1979). "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 1754. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754)

name: Einstein A and B coefficients from detailed balance
summary: Requiring two-level atoms in equilibrium with Planck radiation to obey detailed balance with Boltzmann populations fixes g₁B₁₂ = g₂B₂₁ and A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³; stimulated emission, the source of laser gain, is forced by the Bose–Einstein statistics of photons.

name: Thermal-noise floor of ultrastable reference cavities
summary: Brownian motion of mirror coatings and substrates, computed with the FDT from mechanical loss angles (Levin's direct approach), sets the fundamental stability limit of Fabry–Pérot-stabilized lasers used in optical clocks and gravitational-wave detectors.
sources: Numata, Kemery & Camp (2004). "Thermal-Noise Limit in the Frequency Stabilization of Lasers with Rigid Cavities". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 93, 250602. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.250602](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.250602)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Schawlow–Townes linewidth as phase diffusion
summary: Spontaneous emission kicks the laser phase randomly; above threshold the amplitude is pinned but the phase performs Brownian motion, so the field correlation decays exponentially and the line is a Lorentzian of Schawlow–Townes width, the Langevin/Fokker–Planck laser theory of Lax and Haken.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Laser threshold as a second-order phase transition
summary: Near threshold the single-mode laser field obeys a Langevin equation with a Landau-type potential whose quadratic coefficient changes sign with pump: the field amplitude is an order parameter with mean-field exponent β = 1/2, spontaneous emission is the noise, and the free phase behaves like a Goldstone mode.
map: \dot E=(a-b|E|^2)E+\xi(t)\ \Rightarrow\ V(E)=-\frac a2|E|^2+\frac b4|E|^4,\qquad a\propto P_{\rm pump}-P_{\rm th}
breaks: The laser is a driven-dissipative steady state with no free energy or detailed balance; finite photon number rounds the transition, and the effective temperature is set by spontaneous emission rather than a heat bath.
sources: DeGiorgio & Scully (1970). "Analogy between the Laser Threshold Region and a Second-Order Phase Transition". *Phys. Rev. A* 2, 1170. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.2.1170](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.2.1170)

name: Thermal emission engineering: radiative cooling and TPV
summary: Kirchhoff's law (emissivity equals absorptivity, from detailed balance) lets nanophotonic structures engineer thermal emission: daytime radiative cooling dumps heat into cold space through the 8–13 µm atmospheric window, and selective emitters push thermophotovoltaic conversion toward the Carnot and detailed-balance limits.
map: P_{\rm cool}=P_{\rm rad}(T)-P_{\rm atm}(T_{\rm amb})-P_{\rm sun}-P_{\rm cond},\qquad \epsilon(\lambda,\theta)=\alpha(\lambda,\theta)
sources: Raman et al. (2014). "Passive radiative cooling below ambient air temperature under direct sunlight". *Nature* 515, 540. [doi:10.1038/nature13883](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13883)
Shockley & Queisser (1961). "Detailed Balance Limit of Efficiency of p-n Junction Solar Cells". *J. Appl. Phys.* 32, 510. [doi:10.1063/1.1736034](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1736034)

name: Anderson localization of light
summary: Anderson localization is a wave-interference effect, so it applies to light: John proposed strong photon localization near the band edges of disordered photonic crystals, and transverse localization has been imaged in disordered photonic lattices. Photons have no interactions or Fermi sea, so optics isolates the single-particle physics.
breaks: Absorption mimics localization in transmission measurements, and in 3D dielectrics near-field dipole coupling may prevent true Anderson localization of light.
sources: Anderson (1958). "Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 1492. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492)

name: Fluctuational electrodynamics and near-field heat transfer
summary: Rytov's fluctuational electrodynamics treats thermal emission as Maxwell fields radiated by random currents whose spectrum is fixed by the FDT (∝ Im ε). Between bodies closer than the thermal wavelength, evanescent surface plasmon and phonon polaritons carry heat orders of magnitude beyond the Stefan–Boltzmann limit; the same correlators give Casimir–Lifshitz forces.

name: Coherent Ising machines from degenerate OPOs
summary: A degenerate optical parametric oscillator above threshold settles into one of two phases (0 or π), an optical Ising spin; networks of time-multiplexed OPO pulses with measurement-feedback coupling search for low-energy states of Ising and Sherrington–Kirkpatrick Hamiltonians, using the pitchfork bifurcation as an annealing schedule.

name: Optical thermodynamics of multimode nonlinear fibres
summary: In highly multimode nonlinear waveguides the conserved optical power and Hamiltonian play the roles of particle number and energy; weak Kerr mixing drives modal occupations to a Rayleigh–Jeans distribution with an optical temperature and chemical potential, and beam self-cleaning appears as condensation into the fundamental mode.

name: Optical NLS, inverse scattering and the Bethe ansatz
summary: Pulse propagation in a Kerr fibre obeys the integrable nonlinear Schrödinger equation, solved exactly by inverse scattering; its quantized form is the attractive delta-interacting Bose gas (Lieb–Liniger/McGuire), which Lai and Haus solved by Bethe ansatz to describe quantum optical solitons.

name: Planck's resonators: dipole emission balances absorption

name: Rayleigh–Brillouin spectrum and the dynamic structure factor
summary: Light inelastically scattered by a fluid shows a central Rayleigh line (heat diffusion) and two Brillouin lines (sound); their widths and the Landau–Placzek intensity ratio come from the hydrodynamic dynamic structure factor S(q,ω), which by the FDT is the absorptive part of the density response.

summary: Light scattered by diffusing particles decorrelates as g⁽¹⁾(q,τ) = exp(−Dq²τ); with the Siegert relation and Stokes–Einstein D = k_BT/6πηa, photon-correlation spectroscopy turns Einstein's Brownian-motion theory into a routine size and dynamics probe, extended to multiple scattering by diffusing-wave spectroscopy.

summary: Rayleigh scattering from a fluid measures its density fluctuations, I ∝ S(q) with S(0) = nk_BTκ_T (Einstein–Smoluchowski). Near a critical point κ_T and ξ diverge and the fluid turns milky; the Ornstein–Zernike angular dependence of the scattered light was a primary measurement of γ, ν and η.

name: Classical optics as the coherent-state limit
summary: Classical wave optics is reproduced exactly by quantized light in coherent states: first-order interference, diffraction and imaging depend only on mode functions and the mean field, so quantum features appear only in photon counting and higher-order correlations.

summary: The classical degree of coherence g^(1) and the Hanbury Brown–Twiss intensity correlation g^(2) become Glauber's normally ordered field correlators. Thermal bunching g^(2)(0)=2 appears in both theories; antibunching g^(2)(0)<1 is the purely quantum signature.

name: Hamilton's optico-mechanical analogy: eikonal ↔ action
summary: Fermat's principle and the eikonal equation are the short-wavelength limit of wave optics, just as Hamilton–Jacobi mechanics is the ħ→0 limit of quantum mechanics. Schrödinger built wave mechanics by completing Hamilton's analogy, and WKB semiclassics is the eikonal method applied to matter waves.

name: Atom interferometry: optical interferometers for atoms
summary: Light-pulse atom interferometers copy the Mach–Zehnder geometry, with laser pulses as beam splitters and mirrors, and Ramsey's separated-field method is a two-slit experiment in time. They measure g, rotations and h/m and test the equivalence principle.
breaks: Atoms are massive, with quadratic dispersion and internal states. Their phase picks up gravity and photon recoil, and their beam splitters are coherent internal-state transitions rather than passive optics.

name: Huygens–Fresnel principle as free-particle propagator
summary: Fresnel diffraction sums secondary wavelets weighted by e^{ikr}, just as Feynman's path integral sums e^{iS/ħ}. The paraxial Fresnel kernel is the free-particle propagator with z↔t and k↔m/ħ, and stationary phase picks out rays, the optical counterpart of classical paths.

breaks: The optical 'time' z is a spatial coordinate, and the mapping fails beyond the paraxial, scalar approximation (obliquity factors, vector diffraction).

name: Beam splitters: Mach–Zehnder to Hong–Ou–Mandel
summary: The beam-splitter unitary is the same for classical field amplitudes and for photon creation operators, so a single photon reproduces classical fringes. Two identical photons bunch (the HOM dip) with visibility up to 100% against a classical maximum of 50%, which is how single-photon sources are certified as indistinguishable.
breaks: Two-photon interference depends on number states and photon indistinguishability; no classical field gives HOM visibility above 50%.
sources: Hong, Ou & Mandel (1987). "Measurement of subpicosecond time intervals between two photons by interference". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 59, 2044. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.2044](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.2044)

name: Interferometer shot noise and squeezed-vacuum injection
summary: With coherent light, a Michelson or Mach–Zehnder interferometer's phase sensitivity is shot-noise limited at 1/√N. Caves showed this noise enters as vacuum fluctuations through the unused port, so injecting squeezed vacuum there beats the limit, as LIGO and Virgo now do.
sources: Caves (1981). "Quantum-mechanical noise in an interferometer". *Phys. Rev. D* 23, 1693. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693)

name: Polarization qubits and polarization entanglement
summary: Jones vectors are qubit states and wave plates are SU(2) gates. Photon pairs entangled in polarization are therefore the main platform for entanglement witnesses, state tomography and Bell tests.

Horodecki et al. (2009). "Quantum entanglement". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 865. [arXiv:quant-ph/0702225](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0702225)

name: Photon spin and orbital angular momentum
summary: Circularly polarized light carries spin angular momentum ±ħ per photon (Beth 1936), and Laguerre–Gauss beams with phase e^{iℓφ} carry orbital angular momentum ℓħ. Transfer to atoms follows the Δm selection rules, and both degrees of freedom serve as qudit encodings.
breaks: The massless photon has only helicity ±1 (no m=0 state), and the split into spin and orbital parts is gauge-dependent outside the paraxial regime.

name: Pancharatnam phase on the Poincaré sphere
summary: Pancharatnam (1956) found that light taken around a closed cycle of polarization states gains a phase of minus half the solid angle it encloses on the Poincaré sphere. This is Berry's spin-1/2 phase, found in optics decades earlier, and it is now used in Pancharatnam–Berry geometric-phase metasurfaces.

name: Polarization coherency matrix = qubit density matrix
summary: The 2×2 coherency matrix of partially polarized light is a density matrix whose Stokes parameters are the Bloch-vector components. The degree of polarization is the Bloch-vector length, wave plates act as unitaries, and depolarizing elements (Mueller matrices) act as quantum channels.
breaks: Classical partial polarization is an ensemble average over field fluctuations; beams that are nonseparable in polarization and spatial mode ('classical entanglement') show no nonlocality.

name: Microwave billiards as quantum-chaos simulators
summary: Below the cutoff of the second vertical mode, a flat microwave cavity's TM modes obey the 2D Helmholtz equation, which is the Schrödinger equation of a particle in a hard-wall billiard. Measured resonance spectra test random-matrix level statistics (GOE for chaotic shapes) and wavefunction scarring.
breaks: Holds only for the lowest TM modes of thin cavities. Absorption broadens the levels, and time reversal can be broken only by adding ferrites.
sources: Bohigas, Giannoni & Schmit (1984). "Characterization of Chaotic Quantum Spectra and Universality of Level Fluctuation Laws". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 52, 1. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1)

name: Transmission-line resonators as circuit-QED cavities
summary: Superconducting coplanar-waveguide resonators, which are classical transmission lines with standing-wave modes, supply the photon modes of circuit QED. Their tiny transverse mode volume makes vacuum fields large enough for a transmon to reach strong coupling.

name: Cavity and waveguide modes become photon modes
summary: To quantize the field, expand it in the classical normal modes of the cavity or waveguide (Helmholtz solutions obeying the boundary conditions) and promote each mode amplitude to a harmonic-oscillator operator. Mode shapes, mode volumes and dispersion carry over unchanged.

name: Field momentum and radiation pressure in optomechanics
summary: The momentum carried by electromagnetic fields (Poynting vector, Maxwell stress tensor) pushes on a reflector with radiation pressure 2P/c. In a cavity this force scales with the intracavity photon number, which gives the optomechanical coupling used to cool, squeeze and entangle mechanical motion.

name: Aharonov–Bohm phase as holonomy of the potential
summary: The vector potential is a U(1) connection: a charge that encircles a flux picks up the phase q∮A·dl/ħ even where B=0. Berry's phase is the same holonomy, taken for a connection on parameter space.

name: Spin–orbit coupling from field transformations
summary: An electron moving through an atom's electric field sees a magnetic field B'=−v×E/c² in its rest frame, which couples to its spin. Relativistic Thomas precession halves the naive result, giving the fine-structure term that the Dirac equation yields directly.

name: Earnshaw's theorem and the RF Paul trap
summary: Laplace's equation rules out a static 3D potential minimum for a charge (Earnshaw's theorem). Ion traps therefore use an oscillating quadrupole whose time-averaged ponderomotive pseudopotential confines the ion, and designing the electrodes is an electrostatic boundary-value problem.
sources: Cirac & Zoller (1995). "Quantum Computations with Cold Trapped Ions". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 74, 4091. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.4091](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.4091)

name: Lorentz oscillator and quantum oscillator strengths
summary: The classical Lorentz model of a bound electron gives the dielectric function and Rayleigh's ω^4 law. Quantum mechanics keeps its form, placing resonances at transition frequencies weighted by oscillator strengths that obey the Thomas–Reiche–Kuhn sum rule. Kramers–Heisenberg dispersion theory led directly to Heisenberg's matrix mechanics.
sources: Heisenberg (1925). "Über quantentheoretische Umdeutung kinematischer und mechanischer Beziehungen". *Z. Phys.* 33, 879. [doi:10.1007/BF01328377](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01328377)

name: Multipole order sets atomic selection rules
summary: Expanding the atom–field coupling in multipoles gives E1, M1, E2… transitions. Their angular-momentum and parity selection rules follow from each multipole's spherical-tensor rank, and each higher order is suppressed by about (ka)^2. The resulting narrow 'forbidden' lines serve as clock transitions.

name: Lasers as the enabling toolkit of AMO physics
summary: Narrow-linewidth, tunable, stabilized lasers made laser cooling, optical trapping, precision spectroscopy and coherent control of atoms possible. In return, atomic references stabilize laser frequencies.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Photonic devices as quantum-optical hardware
summary: The laser is itself a quantum-optical system: spontaneous-emission noise sets its Schawlow–Townes linewidth, and above threshold it emits near-coherent light. Photonic components (nonlinear crystals, waveguides, cavities) are the building blocks of quantum light sources and circuits.

name: Integrated linear optics as photonic quantum processors
summary: Classical integrated-photonics parts (directional couplers, thermo-optic phase shifters, Mach–Zehnder meshes that realize any unitary) become photonic qubit gates. They underpin linear-optical (KLM) and fusion-based architectures and boson-sampling machines.

name: Telecom fibre and photonic chips for QKD
summary: Quantum key distribution and entanglement distribution run on low-loss 1550 nm telecom fibre with integrated transmitters and receivers. Fibre transmission falls exponentially with distance, which caps repeaterless key rates and motivates quantum repeaters.

name: Frequency combs and stabilized lasers for optical clocks
summary: A mode-locked laser's pulse train is a comb of exactly spaced lines that links optical clock transitions to countable microwave frequencies. Pound–Drever–Hall locking to ultrastable cavities gives the sub-hertz-linewidth lasers that interrogate lattice and ion clocks.
sources: Ludlow et al. (2015). "Optical atomic clocks". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 87, 637. [arXiv:1407.3493](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.3493)

name: Laser radiation pressure: Doppler cooling and traps
summary: A narrow-linewidth laser tuned below resonance exerts a velocity-dependent scattering force that Doppler-cools atoms to T_D=ħΓ/2k_B. Intense far-detuned beams instead give conservative dipole potentials, the basis of optical traps and tweezers.
sources: Ashkin (1970). "Acceleration and Trapping of Particles by Radiation Pressure". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 24, 156. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156)

name: Optical resonators: laser cavity to strong coupling
summary: The Fabry–Pérot resonator that gives a laser its feedback becomes, at small mode volume and high finesse, a cavity where one atom and one photon exchange energy faster than either decays. The same Q/V figure of merit sets the Purcell factor.
sources: Jaynes & Cummings (1963). "Comparison of quantum and semiclassical radiation theories with application to the beam maser". *Proc. IEEE* 51, 89. [doi:10.1109/PROC.1963.1664](https://doi.org/10.1109/PROC.1963.1664)

name: Einstein A/B and laser photon statistics
summary: Einstein's A/B ratio, derived from Planck's law, says spontaneous emission is stimulated emission driven by the vacuum's one photon per mode. Below threshold a laser emits thermal-like light with g^(2)(0)=2; above threshold its output is near-Poissonian coherent light with g^(2)(0)→1.

name: Superconducting circuits as microwave metamaterials
summary: Josephson-junction arrays and high-kinetic-inductance lines are lumped-element metamaterials with engineered dispersion. Dispersion engineering (band gaps, resonant phase matching) underlies Josephson travelling-wave parametric amplifiers, Purcell filters and band-gap waveguides coupled to transmons.

name: Photonic band gaps and nanocavities in cavity QED
summary: A photonic band gap suppresses spontaneous emission by removing optical modes. Photonic-crystal and plasmonic nanocavities with tiny mode volumes enhance it (Purcell effect) and reach strong coupling with single quantum dots or molecules: cavity QED in engineered media.

name: Kerr NLSE in fibres ↔ Gross–Pitaevskii equation
summary: Pulses in a Kerr fibre and a BEC's mean-field dynamics obey the same cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Bright and dark solitons, modulational instability, self-focusing collapse and four-wave mixing all have matter-wave counterparts, and 'fluids of light' show superfluid-like flow.

name: Josephson junctions as microwave Kerr nonlinearities
summary: The Josephson cosine potential is a lossless microwave nonlinearity: expanded about its minimum, its quartic Kerr term makes the transmon an anharmonic oscillator. Pumped junctions work as parametric amplifiers and frequency converters, carrying four-wave mixing, phase matching and squeezing over to circuits.

name: SPDC: heralded single photons and entangled pairs
summary: Spontaneous parametric down-conversion is vacuum-seeded χ(2) difference-frequency generation: a pump photon splits into signal and idler photons, with phase matching enforcing energy and momentum conservation. Detecting one photon heralds the other, and type-II phase matching yields polarization-entangled pairs.

name: Parametric down-conversion as a squeezing source
summary: A degenerate χ(2) parametric amplifier (an OPO below threshold) produces squeezed vacuum through its two-photon Hamiltonian, and Kerr χ(3) media also squeeze. These sources are now injected into gravitational-wave interferometers.
map: H=\frac{i\hbar\kappa}{2}(\hat a^{\dagger2}-\hat a^2)\Rightarrow\Delta X_{\rm sq}=\tfrac12e^{-r},\ \Delta X_{\rm anti}=\tfrac12e^{r},\ r=\kappa t
sources: Caves (1981). "Quantum-mechanical noise in an interferometer". *Phys. Rev. D* 23, 1693. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693)

name: Helical waveguide arrays as Floquet topological insulators
summary: In coupled waveguide arrays the paraxial equation makes propagation distance z act as time. Helically modulated waveguides therefore form a periodically driven lattice whose Floquet bands carry (anomalous) topology and chiral edge states, Floquet engineering demonstrated first with light.
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Gain/loss photonics: PT symmetry and exceptional points
summary: Optical lattices and resonators with engineered gain and loss are the main experimental platform for PT-symmetric Hamiltonians, exceptional points, the non-Hermitian skin effect and topological lasers. There the paraxial wave equation plays the role of a Schrödinger equation with a complex potential.
sources: Bender & Boettcher (1998). "Real Spectra in Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians Having PT Symmetry". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 80, 5243. [arXiv:physics/9712001](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/9712001)
Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Berry curvature and Chern numbers of photonic bands
summary: Bloch modes of photonic crystals carry the same Berry connection and curvature as electronic bands. Breaking time reversal with magneto-optic media gives nonzero Chern numbers and chiral, backscattering-immune edge modes.
map: \mathcal A_n=i\langle u_{n\mathbf k}|\nabla_{\mathbf k}u_{n\mathbf k}\rangle_\epsilon,\ C=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\rm BZ}\Omega\,d^2k\in\mathbb Z,\ N_{\rm edge}=\Delta C
breaks: The photonic inner product is ε-weighted, and with no Fermi level there is no quantized Hall conductance, only bulk–edge mode counting.

name: High-harmonic generation as a sum over quantum orbits
summary: The three-step recollision model of HHG is a semiclassical evaluation of the strong-field path integral. Saddle points of the action give complex 'quantum orbits' whose classical return energy produces the I_p+3.17U_p cutoff, and the imaginary part of the ionization time encodes tunnelling.
sources: Krausz & Ivanov (2009). "Attosecond physics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 163. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.81.163](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.81.163)
Paul et al. (2001). "Observation of a Train of Attosecond Pulses from High Harmonic Generation". *Science* 292, 1689. [doi:10.1126/science.1059413](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1059413)

name: Cherenkov emission and the Landau critical velocity
summary: A source moving faster than the phase velocity of a medium's waves radiates them (Cherenkov emission). The Landau criterion for superfluidity is the same kinematic condition for emitting Bogoliubov excitations, so an obstacle dragged through a BEC faster than v_c≈c_s leaves a Cherenkov-like phonon wake.
breaks: The Bogoliubov dispersion is nonlinear, so the threshold is min ε/p rather than a constant phase velocity and the wake is not a simple cone. In practice, vortex nucleation sets a lower critical velocity.

name: Larmor dipole power ↔ Einstein A coefficient
summary: An atomic transition's spontaneous-emission rate equals the classical Larmor power of a dipole oscillating with amplitude 2|d_12|, divided by ħω. This is the correspondence principle at its sharpest, and it fixes natural linewidths and lifetimes.
breaks: A classical dipole decays continuously; quantum emission happens in discrete jumps, needs vacuum fluctuations to start from an energy eigenstate, and never occurs from the ground state.

name: Purcell effect: classical dipole power = quantum rate
summary: At weak coupling, any photonic environment changes a quantum emitter's decay rate by exactly the factor it changes a classical dipole's radiated power. Both are set by the local density of optical states (the dyadic Green's function), which guides nanoantenna and cavity design for bright single-photon sources.
map: \frac{\Gamma}{\Gamma_0}=\frac{P}{P_0}=\frac{6\pi c}{\omega}\,\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathrm{Im}\,\mathbf G(\mathbf r_0,\mathbf r_0;\omega)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}
breaks: Fails at strong coupling (vacuum Rabi splitting, non-exponential decay) and says nothing about photon statistics.
